docs.title: FAQ
docs.text: Short answers to questions people ask about Kitsune, with links to the details.

docs.title: How is it different from Playwright MCP?
docs.text:
Playwright MCP launches and drives its own browser, which suits testing and automation. Kitsune attaches to the Firefox, Zen or LibreWolf window you already use and is built to share it with you: agent tabs open in the background, writes to the tab you are using are held, and closing your tabs needs a separate confirmation step.

By default Kitsune publishes Playwright MCP's 25 core tools with the same names, descriptions and schemas, so prompts written for Playwright MCP carry over. On shared-browser tasks it kept the user's tab in front in 23 of 24 tasks, against 2 of 24 for Playwright MCP, which was not designed to share a browser with a person. See the benchmark and Positioning.

docs.title: How is it different from Mozilla's Firefox DevTools MCP?
docs.text: Firefox DevTools MCP is the stronger choice for debugging and profiling, and attaches to a Firefox started with remote-debugging flags. Kitsune connects through an extension and a local bridge, so your normal profile needs no startup flags or WebDriver, and it concentrates on working alongside you rather than on developer tooling.

docs.title: Does it work with Chrome or other Chromium browsers?
docs.text: Not yet. A Chromium version is planned, probably as a separate project. For Chrome today, a Chromium extension MCP such as Browser MCP fits better.

docs.title: Which agents can use it?
docs.text: Any MCP client that runs local stdio servers. The installation page has setup for Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, Claude Desktop and Cursor: Register the MCP server.

docs.title: Will the agent take over the tab I'm using?
docs.text: Tabs it opens with browser_tabs new stay in the background, and selecting a tab changes only the agent's current tab, not what you see. Until the agent opens or selects a tab, its reads act on the tab you are viewing, and its writes and navigations that name no tab fail with no_current_tab. The agent can read every tab, and select any of them to read it. Your tabs and other clients' tabs are read-only by default, whether viewed or in the background: writes, navigation, scrolling and closing fail immediately with user_tab_read_only, without a prompt. The agent should open its own tab first. Trusted input still pauses writes on an agent tab with user_active. For the permission opt-out, see Protecting your tabs. OS-level clicks and popups that sites open can still take focus; see Shared browser.

docs.title: Can I limit what the agent does?
docs.text:
Yes, in three ways that combine:

  • KITSUNE_MODE=read, draft or act limits both the tools the agent sees and the requests the bridge accepts. Draft fills supported fields but has no click or submit tools. See Task modes.
  • KITSUNE_CAPS enables tool groups; the default is the 25 core tools, browser_resume and browser_ask_user. Groups that read personal data (storage, history) must be named. See Tools, capabilities and modes.
  • Ask-before-act holds submits, payment pages, JavaScript and cookie access until you approve.

docs.title: How do I approve a held action?
docs.text: An ask-before-act hold returns needs_user and does not run the held action (#376). User-tab writes are refused without prompting; an explicit handoff request asks in the browser first, then falls back to the client. For ask-before-act on an MCP client with elicitation (Claude Code, Codex), the client asks you in its own prompt, naming the action, its target and the tab; Approve runs that one call, and the agent never sees the approval. Clients without elicitation fall back to a confirmation token (confirm_token): the agent should ask you, then repeat the call with it. Either way the bridge's audit log records how each write was approved. See Approving held actions.

docs.title: What happens when the agent needs me?
docs.text: For a sign-in, a CAPTCHA, a button that ignores the agent's clicks or a choice only you can make, the agent asks you with browser_ask_user: in the client's prompt (Done or Can't) where it has elicitation, else in its reply. In the reply case, for a sign-in or CAPTCHA Kitsune sees on the tab, browser_resume waits until it is gone, so you need not tell the agent you are done. See When the agent needs you.

docs.title: Is it safe to give an agent my browser?
docs.text: Treat it as giving the agent your signed-in accounts. None of Kitsune's controls prevent prompt injection: a page can contain text that steers the agent. Approval in the client's prompt (elicitation) does not pass through the agent, but the confirmation token, the fallback for clients without elicitation, proves a second step, not that a person approved. Use a dedicated browser profile, give it only the accounts the task needs, and have the agent ask you before it sends, buys or deletes anything. See Security.

docs.title: Does my data leave my machine?
docs.text: The bridge listens only on 127.0.0.1, requires a token, and accepts the WebSocket only from the extension. Page content you let the agent read goes to your agent, and from there to whichever model provider that agent uses.

docs.title: Do I need the developer build of the extension?
docs.text: Only for agent-supplied JavaScript (browser_evaluate). The signed build installs once and updates itself; the developer build is a temporary add-on that you load again after a browser restart. See Installation.

docs.title: Which platforms are supported?
docs.text: macOS and Linux. Windows has not been tested since the fork. OS-level trusted clicks work on macOS, Windows and Linux under X11, not Wayland. See Requirements.

docs.title: Why can't the agent open "Continue with Google" and other sign-in popups?
docs.text: Kitsune's clicks are synthetic DOM events without user activation, and with its default popup blocker Firefox opens OAuth/SSO popups only from a real click, so the popup is blocked or the site shows an error. When the site's script calls window.open during the click and the popup is refused, the click result has a popup_blocked warning with state.reason: "script_popup"; other failures give no warning. The recommended fallback is to have the agent ask you to click the button, then continue in the popup or tab that opens; this keeps your pointer and focus yours. browser_trusted_click sends a real OS click instead. On macOS it needs uvx --from 'kitsune-browser-mcp[macos]' kitsune or brew install cliclick, Accessibility permission for the app running the bridge, and kitsune-bridge stop so the next start picks the change up. The bridge runs with the Python and PATH of whichever MCP server started it first. See Sign-in popups (OAuth/SSO).

docs.title: Is this the same project as kitsune-mcp?
docs.text: No. kitsune-mcp on PyPI and kaiser-data/kitsune-mcp are unrelated projects. This one is published as kitsune-browser-mcp and in the MCP Registry as io.github.junyeong-nero/kitsune.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
agent ──stdio──▶ kitsune (MCP server, one per agent)
                    │ HTTP 127.0.0.1:47651 + bearer token
                    ▼
                 bridge daemon (one per user, started on demand)
                    │ WebSocket 127.0.0.1:47652, moz-extension:// origin only
                    ▼
                 Kitsune extension ──▶ tabs (content scripts)
  1. The agent launches kitsune over stdio.
  2. If no bridge is answering, kitsune spawns python -m kitsune.bridge as a detached daemon. If its build differs, Kitsune safely replaces it first. A file lock serializes starts and replacements across agents.
  3. The extension keeps reconnecting to the daemon, so it attaches by itself. After kitsune starts or replaces a daemon, its first tool call other than browser_status waits up to 16 s for the extension; it is sent once either way.
  4. The daemon keeps running after the agent exits; the next agent reuses it.

docs.title: Snapshot and element refs
docs.text:
Start with browser_snapshot(tab_id=...) to get a compact accessibility-style text tree of visible controls, headings, and landmarks:

- main ""
  - heading "Welcome" [ref=e0] [level=1]
  - button "Log in" [ref=e1]

Prefer browser_click(ref="e1", element="Log in", tab_id=...) and browser_type(ref="...", text="...", mode="fill", tab_id=...). element is a description for audit logs only; CSS selector remains supported. For drag, use ref for the source and to_ref for the destination (or the existing selector arguments). A write action's selector must match one element: several matches fail with ambiguous_target and act on nothing, unless first=True (see Strict selectors). This includes trusted clicks, focus/blur, targeted scrolling, fuzzy form-fill keys, and uploads without a selector on pages with several file inputs. Ambiguous clicks fail before ask-before-act offers confirmation.

Short refs (e12) name attached nodes in one tab/document, tracked by the extension. New snapshots, browser_dom, find and full or delta post-action observations reuse those refs; an unchanged attached node keeps its ref even if its name or position changes. Detachment/replacement, frame-document retirement, navigation or content reinjection invalidates the old identity. Indexes are never reused across observations or tabs; after an extension reload, take a new snapshot. A stale ref reports element_removed, not_in_snapshot (never issued/unknown), or other_document in state.reason. An other_document error names the one element of the targeted page with the ref's role and name, if there is exactly one, in state.same_element; nothing is done to it. Take a new scoped observation of the intended tab; never repeat a write merely to refresh refs. Earlier attached refs remain usable without another observation.

Click, type, fill, select, check, keypress, submit, and navigate responses include a snapshot capped at 4,000 characters (snapshot_truncated indicates more content; snapshot_hint gives scope guidance and explains if the target/context could not fit). target_ref, when included, is the acted-on element's ref for a follow-up action. For click, type, fill, select, check and keypress it is a delta (snapshot_delta: true): only the target and what the action changed or revealed, such as an opened menu's options, anchored there instead of at the page top, and a - removed: … line for each part it closed or removed, such as a dialog (#457), folded into one counted line when more than three share a parent (#471); earlier refs stay valid. A click or hover that opens a menu, listbox or dialog also returns opened_popup: its ref, the ref of the control that opened it (opened_by) and its items' refs, also when a background tab did not paint it (rendered: false; see Opened popups). Submit, navigate and actions that load another document return a full snapshot (see Post-action snapshots). If snapshot capture fails, snapshot_error preserves the action result; take a new snapshot before using refs. To recover from a stale ref, take a new snapshot and retry with the new ref; never repeat a write just to refresh refs. See Ref lifetime for the full contract and MCP error results for which results are returned with isError: true. For reading tasks, browser_snapshot(text=True) also returns visible text lines, URL, title and tab ID in one bounded call (see browser_snapshot). To start a task, browser_tabs(include_active=True) returns the tab list with that read of the active tab as active_page. Set KITSUNE_POST_ACTION_SNAPSHOT=0 in the bridge daemon's environment and restart the daemon to disable these automatic snapshots, or full to always return full ones. Explicit snapshots remain available. This is a DOM-based accessibility approximation, not Firefox's platform accessibility tree; open and closed shadow roots are traversed. Same-origin iframes are read and acted on like the page. browser_snapshot, browser_find, browser_forms, browser_dom and post-action deltas also read the content of cross-origin iframes (embedded payment forms, sign-in widgets, players), whose refs clicks, typing and trusted clicks accept (see Frames).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Kitsune has two parts that you install separately:

  1. The MCP server. Your MCP client launches it over stdio. You register it once with a command; uv downloads and runs it, so you do not need a checkout.
  2. The browser extension. You install it in your browser yourself. The browser asks for your approval, and nothing is installed silently.

The server starts the shared bridge daemon on demand. The extension connects to that daemon by itself once both are installed.

  • Prerequisites
  • 1. Register the MCP server
  • 2. Install the browser extension
  • 3. Check the connection
  • Pinning a version
  • Upgrading
  • Automatic extension updates
  • Extension and server compatibility

Setup problems are covered in Troubleshooting. To run Kitsune from a checkout, see Development.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• uv, which provides uvx. uv downloads a supported Python (3.10+) if none is installed.
  • Git, only if you install from the Git source instead of PyPI (see Pinning a version).
  • A Firefox-family browser, Gecko 142+: Firefox 142+, Zen 1.23+, or LibreWolf.
  • macOS or Linux. Windows is untested.

docs.title: 1. Register the MCP server
docs.text:
Every client runs the same stdio command:

uvx --from kitsune-browser-mcp kitsune

The first start downloads Kitsune and its dependencies into the uv cache, which takes a few seconds. Later starts reuse the cached version until you upgrade (see Upgrading). Kitsune is published on PyPI as kitsune-browser-mcp; kitsune-mcp is an unrelated project, so do not install that name.

On macOS, browser_trusted_click (needed for example to open "Continue with Google" popups) needs uvx --from 'kitsune-browser-mcp[macos]' kitsune or brew install cliclick, plus Accessibility permission; see Sign-in popups.

Optionally, warm the cache and check the install before you register it:

uvx --from kitsune-browser-mcp kitsune-bridge status

This prints {"status": "stopped"} (or the running bridge's status) and never starts a daemon. Running kitsune with --help does not print help: it is the MCP server itself, starts the bridge, and waits for an MCP client on stdin.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
claude mcp add --scope user kitsune -- uvx --from kitsune-browser-mcp kitsune

--scope user makes Kitsune available in every project. Leave it out to register it only for the current project (local scope). Pass environment variables with -e, for example -e KITSUNE_CAPS=core,network before the --.

docs.title: Codex CLI
docs.text:
codex mcp add kitsune -- uvx --from kitsune-browser-mcp kitsune

or in ~/.codex/config.toml:

[mcp_servers.kitsune]
command = "uvx"
args = ["--from", "kitsune-browser-mcp", "kitsune"]

# Optional
[mcp_servers.kitsune.env]
KITSUNE_CAPS = "core,network"

docs.title: Pi
docs.text:
With Pi's built-in MCP support:

pi mcp add kitsune -- uvx --from kitsune-browser-mcp kitsune
pi mcp list

This writes user-level configuration to ~/.pi/agent/mcp.json. Add --local before kitsune to write .pi/mcp.json in the current project instead; project configuration is loaded only after project trust is granted. In a running session, use /reload to pick up the change and /mcp to inspect the connection.

You can also edit the JSON config directly using the mcpServers example below. If an MCP adapter extension overrides built-in MCP support, use that extension's configuration instructions instead.

docs.title: Claude Desktop, Cursor, Pi, and other mcpServers clients
docs.text:
Edit the client's JSON config, for example ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json (Claude Desktop on macOS), ~/.cursor/mcp.json or .cursor/mcp.json (Cursor), or ~/.pi/agent/mcp.json or .pi/mcp.json (Pi's built-in MCP support). Merge the entry with any existing servers:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kitsune": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["--from", "kitsune-browser-mcp", "kitsune"]
    }
  }
}

Add an "env": {"KITSUNE_CAPS": "core,network"} object next to args to set environment variables.

docs.title: OpenCode
docs.text:
Edit ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json (global) or opencode.json at a git repo root (project) by hand.

{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "mcp": {
    "kitsune": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["uvx", "--from", "kitsune-browser-mcp", "kitsune"],
      "enabled": true
    }
  }
}

docs.title: GUI apps and PATH
docs.text:
GUI apps such as Claude Desktop often do not inherit your shell PATH. If the client cannot find uvx, use the full path from which uvx as the command, for example /Users/you/.local/bin/uvx. Config files do not expand ~.

Several clients can be configured at once; they share one bridge daemon. Register them all with the same source and ref (see compatibility).

docs.title: 2. Install the browser extension
docs.text:
The extension is not part of the Python package, so download it separately, for the same version as the server. There are two builds:

Signed build (kitsune-<version>.xpi) Developer build (kitsune-extension-dev-<version>.zip) Install Once; survives browser restarts Temporary add-on; load it again after every restart Signed by Mozilla Yes (self-distributed, not listed on AMO) No browser_evaluate, JS conditions in browser_sync_barrier and batch if/while, HTML mode of editable typing, bundled workflows that use js steps Not available Available Everything else Available Available

The signed build cannot run JavaScript supplied by the agent, because Mozilla's add-on policies forbid executing code that is not part of the signed package. Those tools return an error that names the developer build. browser_status (in the admin group, KITSUNE_CAPS=core,admin) reports which build is connected (extension_build: signed or dev).

docs.title: Signed build (recommended)
docs.text:
Signed XPIs are attached to releases from 0.2.0 on. For 0.1.0, use the developer build below.

  1. Download kitsune-<version>.xpi from GitHub Releases.
  2. Open about:addons, click the gear icon, choose Install Add-on From File…, and select the XPI. Dragging the file onto a browser window also works.
  3. Approve the permission prompt. The browser asks every time; nothing is installed silently.
  4. Restart or reconnect your MCP client and ask it to list your tabs (browser_tabs with action: "list"). With admin enabled, browser_status should report "extension_connected": true and "extension_build": "signed".

Signed builds released after 0.2.0 update themselves (see Automatic extension updates).

docs.title: Developer build
docs.text:
Use this for browser_evaluate, or to run an unreleased commit.

  1. Download kitsune-extension-dev-<version>.zip from GitHub Releases and unzip it. For 0.1.0 the file is named kitsune-extension-0.1.0.zip. For an unreleased commit, use the extension/ folder of a repository ZIP or clone.
  2. Open about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox and click Load Temporary Add-on….
  3. Select manifest.json from the unzipped folder (extension/manifest.json in a repository ZIP or clone). In the macOS file dialog, press Cmd+Shift+G to paste a path.
  4. With admin enabled, call browser_status; it should report "extension_build": "dev".

Both builds use the same add-on ID. While a developer build is loaded, it replaces the signed one; after a browser restart the signed build is back.

docs.title: 3. Check the connection
docs.text: Restart the agent and ask it to list your tabs (browser_tabs with action: "list"). An error's hint says what to fix; with KITSUNE_CAPS=core,admin, browser_status reports "extension_connected": true and a full diagnosis. Then try a first task.

docs.title: Pinning a version
docs.text:
Pin a released version with ==:

claude mcp add --scope user kitsune -- uvx --from kitsune-browser-mcp==0.7.3 kitsune

Releases are listed on PyPI and GitHub Releases, which also carries the matching signed XPI and developer-build zip.

To run a commit, tag, or branch that is not on PyPI, use the Git source with @<ref> (requires Git). The MCP server's package is in packages/kitsune-browser-mcp; uv builds the code it depends on, kitsune-browser, from the same ref:

claude mcp add --scope user kitsune -- uvx --from "git+https://github.com/junyeong-nero/kitsune.git@<ref>#subdirectory=packages/kitsune-browser-mcp" kitsune

Without @<ref>, the Git source follows the latest default-branch commit. Get the extension from the same ref: https://github.com/junyeong-nero/kitsune/archive/<ref>.zip, or git checkout <ref> in a clone.

docs.title: Server
docs.text:
• Unpinned PyPI (--from kitsune-browser-mcp): uvx keeps using the cached version. To move to the newest release, refresh it once, then restart or reconnect the MCP client (in Claude Code, /mcp): 
    uvx --refresh --from kitsune-browser-mcp kitsune-bridge status
    To check for a new release on every start instead, register --from kitsune-browser-mcp@latest.
  • Pinned (==<version> or Git @<ref>): change the version in the client config. For Claude Code, run claude mcp remove --scope user kitsune, then run the claude mcp add command again with the new version.
  • Unpinned Git source: uv checks for the latest default-branch commit each time the MCP server starts (observed with uv 0.7.20).
  • A pip install of 0.6.0 or earlier, such as a virtual environment for the Python API: until 0.6.0 kitsune-browser-mcp held the code that kitsune-browser holds now. pip installs kitsune-browser first and then removes the old kitsune-browser-mcp with the files they share, so import kitsune fails afterwards. Restore them once with pip install --force-reinstall --no-deps kitsune-browser. The same holds after pip uninstall kitsune-browser-mcp in an environment that kept 0.6.0. uv and uvx are not affected.
  • A checkout: run git pull, then uv sync.

docs.title: Bridge
docs.text:
Reconnect or restart the MCP server after upgrading it. It compares the running bridge's build (package version plus a source hash, including extension JS/JSON in a checkout) with its own and automatically restarts an outdated bridge. This briefly interrupts all clients sharing that bridge. Set KITSUNE_NO_BRIDGE_RESTART=1 in the MCP server's environment to opt out of automatic replacement. You can also stop it explicitly; the next MCP connection starts a fresh daemon:

uvx --from kitsune-browser-mcp kitsune-bridge status  # JSON; includes bridge_version and build
uvx --from kitsune-browser-mcp kitsune-bridge stop

From a checkout, use uv run kitsune-bridge status / stop instead. Plain kitsune-bridge (or kitsune-bridge start) still runs the daemon in the foreground. status and stop never start a daemon. All commands use the same KITSUNE_HOME, token, and port environment settings as the server.

Shutdown uses a token-authenticated endpoint, with a verified, locked PID file as the termination fallback; it never uses a broad pkill. Very old daemons that have neither the shutdown endpoint nor a PID file require a one-time manual stop of the specific old bridge process. Kitsune reports this instead of guessing a PID or launching another daemon over it. After that, automatic replacement and kitsune-bridge stop work normally.

docs.title: Extension
docs.text:
Update the extension to the same version as the server: the signed build updates itself (see Automatic extension updates); for 0.2.0, or to update right away, install the new release's XPI the same way as the first time (it replaces the old version and keeps no separate copy). For the developer build, load the new release and click Reload on Kitsune in about:debugging (or load the updated manifest.json again). A bridge restart reconnects the extension but does not reload its browser-side code; reload it explicitly after extension updates, and reload existing tabs if their content scripts are still outdated. browser_status reports a developer build whose files changed after it was loaded as extension_version_mismatch (state.reason: "stale_developer_build").

Then reconnect the MCP client again if needed (in Claude Code, use /mcp to reconnect Kitsune), and call browser_status. Check extension_connected, bridge_version, and build.

docs.title: Idle shutdown (opt-in)
docs.text:
By default the shared bridge keeps running until it is stopped. To have it exit when no client has used it for a while, set KITSUNE_BRIDGE_IDLE_TIMEOUT (in seconds) in the MCP server's environment, or run the daemon yourself with kitsune-bridge start --idle-timeout SECONDS. 0 (the default) disables it.

  • Every HTTP call to the bridge counts as activity; MCP servers make one per tool call. The extension's WebSocket connection does not count.
  • The timer only runs while nothing is in flight: no HTTP request, no command waiting on the extension, and no browser_keep_alive loop. Call browser_keep_alive_stop when you no longer need one, or the bridge never goes idle.
  • The next tool call from any client starts a fresh bridge automatically. While an idle bridge is exiting, a client that needs one waits for it to finish instead of racing it.
  • The bridge is shared, so the first MCP server that starts it decides the timeout; the setting in other clients takes effect the next time they start it.

docs.title: Automatic extension updates
docs.text:
The signed build checks https://github.com/junyeong-nero/kitsune/releases/latest/download/updates.json and installs the signed XPI of the latest release. This works from the release after 0.2.0 on: the 0.2.0 XPI has no update URL, so install the next release's XPI once by hand (see Signed build); later releases then arrive automatically. The developer build never updates itself.

  • The browser checks about once a day. To check now, open about:addons, click the gear icon, and choose Check for Updates. Updates can be turned off per add-on on Kitsune's page in about:addons (Allow automatic updates).
  • A release's updates.json is published only after its server is on PyPI, but uvx keeps using its cached server (see Upgrading). Until you refresh it, the extension can be newer than the server; browser_status then reports an extension_version that differs from bridge_version.
  • If you pin an older server version, turn off automatic updates for Kitsune and install the matching XPI from that release.

docs.title: Extension and server compatibility
docs.text:
• The server and the extension are developed in the same repository and are only tested together at the same commit. Install both from the same release (or ref). There is no separate compatibility matrix yet.
  • browser_status reports the bridge's bridge_version (package version) and build (package version plus a hash of the bridge code). An installed package does not contain the extension, so its build does not change when only extension files change. Reload the extension yourself after updating it.
  • Use one install source for all clients. A checkout run (uv run --directory …) also hashes the checkout's extension/ files, so its build differs from a uvx install of the same commit. If clients with different builds share a bridge, each one replaces the bridge when it starts. If you need to mix sources, set KITSUNE_NO_BRIDGE_RESTART=1 in the MCP server environments and manage the bridge with kitsune-bridge stop.
  • browser_status also reports the connected extension's extension_version and extension_build. If extension_version differs from bridge_version, upgrade the server (the signed extension updates itself, so it is usually the newer one) or install the matching extension.
  • Browsers: Gecko 142+ (Firefox 142+, Zen 1.23+, LibreWolf). Firefox release and beta builds install only signed extensions, which is why the developer build is a temporary add-on.

docs.title: Philosophy
docs.text: Two principles decide Kitsune's trade-offs. When a feature, default, or fix conflicts with them, the principles win.

docs.title: 1. The user's browser belongs to the user
docs.text:
Kitsune runs inside a browser someone is actively using. The agent is a guest in that workspace, not its owner.

We do:

  • Open agent work in background tabs and leave the user's view where it is.
  • Hold writes to a tab the user is using instead of racing their input.
  • Treat user-owned tabs, focus, and input as off-limits unless the user authorizes otherwise.
  • Prefer refusing with guidance over silently acting somewhere else.

We don't:

  • Trade workspace interference for task speed or benchmark wins.
  • Promise "never interrupts." Where a protection has limits, we document them.

docs.title: 2. Fewer, sharper tools
docs.text:
Every tool, parameter, and description line is paid for in agent context on every call. A larger catalog is a cost, not a feature.

We do:

  • Keep the default surface small and make each tool's contract precise.
  • Enforce delegation limits (read, draft, act) in the system, not in prompts.
  • Report what happened—dispatched, observed, or unknown—and leave the decision to the agent.
  • Add a tool or field only when it removes more agent work than it adds.

We don't:

  • Compete on tool count or copy adjacent tools' catalogs.
  • Fix agent misuse by adding more description text when a simpler contract would prevent it.

For market context and competitor comparison, see Positioning.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
The kitsune package drives the browser you already have open from Python, through the same extension and bridge as the MCP server. The two have different jobs:

  • The MCP server gives an agent a small, curated tool surface. KITSUNE_CAPS, KITSUNE_PUBLISH and KITSUNE_MODE limit what it sees and what the bridge accepts from it.
  • The Python API reaches every capability of the extension and bridge, for scripts and for your own agent frameworks. Its requests carry no capability header, so every group is available, storage and history included.

Both are clients of one shared bridge, and the bridge's shared-browser rules hold for both: tabs open in the background, writes wait while you are using a tab, your own tabs close only with your approval, and sensitive fields are redacted. Ask-before-act, when it is on, holds the same actions.

pip install kitsune-browser      # or: uv add kitsune-browser

kitsune-browser is the code; the MCP server's package, kitsune-browser-mcp, installs it with the mcp extra. Keep a script on the version your MCP clients run, since they share one bridge (Connecting). It needs the Kitsune extension installed in Firefox, Zen or LibreWolf (Installation).

import kitsune

browser = kitsune.connect()                        # starts the bridge if none runs
tab = browser.new_tab("https://news.ycombinator.com")   # a background tab you don't see
for link in tab.query(".titleline > a", fields=["text", "href"], limit=3):
    print(link["text"], link["href"])
tab.close()

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
kitsune.connect() starts the shared bridge if none runs, waits for the extension to reconnect to a bridge it started, and raises ConnectionFailed if the extension is not connected. It returns a Browser.

Argument Default Effect mode "act" "read" or "draft" restricts requests as KITSUNE_MODE does for MCP user_tabs unset (read-only) writable allows this client to write user tabs. See User-tab setting confirm None A function that decides on actions ask-before-act holds; see Ask-before-act replace_bridge False True replaces a running bridge of another build

KITSUNE_HTTP_PORT, KITSUNE_TOKEN and KITSUNE_HOME choose the bridge, as for the MCP server (Configuration).

A script and your MCP clients share the bridge, so they should run the same Kitsune version from the same source. A bridge of another build raises ConnectionFailed with code bridge_version_mismatch and keeps running. The MCP server would replace it, but replacing a bridge drops its clients' keep-alives, intercepts and resume checkpoints, so the Python API does that only with replace_bridge=True (or after kitsune-bridge stop).

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
Browser method Returns tabs() Every open tab: id, url, title, active, windowId, index, owned (this client owns it) new_tab(url="about:blank", wait=True, timeout=15000) A Tab for a new background tab. A load past timeout ms raises TimedOut; the tab stays open, with its id in error.result["tabId"] tab(tab_id) A Tab for an existing tab active_tab() The tab you are viewing. With several windows, each has one: it raises ambiguous_target, and you pick one from tabs()

A Tab sends its id with every request, so it acts on that tab whether or not you are viewing it.

Tab method Does close(force=False) Close this client's tab; user and other clients' tabs are refused with user_tab_read_only by default. force disarms beforeunload show() Switch your view to the tab; call it only when you want that wake() Reload a tab the browser discarded and wait until the page answers duplicate() A Tab for a background copy pin(pinned=True), mute(muted=True), zoom(), set_zoom(factor) Tab state move(window_id=None, index=-1), detach(), resize_window(width, height) Place the tab, give it a window of its own, or resize its window tag(name) Name the tab; browser.tags.tab(name) finds it, .list() and .remove(name) manage names

browser.windows has list(), create(url=None, incognito=False), close(window_id) and focus(window_id), which takes your focus. Closing or focusing a window with user or other clients' tabs is refused by default. browser.pool keeps reusable background tabs: create(size, url), acquire() for a Tab, release(tab).

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
Tab method Returns text() The visible text, as str snapshot(target=None, max_depth=None, text=False) The accessibility-style tree with element refs (e12), as str (Snapshots) markdown(target=None) The page, or one subtree, as Markdown html(target) One element's outerHTML ("html" for the whole page) query(selector, fields=None, limit=50) Fields of every element matching a CSS selector, as a list find(query) Elements matching a description such as "login button", best first, each with a ref forms() Every form field with its label and value links(internal_only=False) The page's links info() URL, title, readyState, sizes, scroll position and recent dialogs screenshot(path=None, target=None, full_page=False, format="png") PNG or JPEG bytes, also written to path. No capture shows the tab evaluate(function, target=None) The JSON value a JavaScript function returns, for example evaluate("() => document.title") or evaluate("el => el.value", "e3"). Needs the developer extension build dom(target=None, max_depth=None) The accessibility tree of interactive elements, as nested dicts images(), iframes() The page's images and frames, as lists meta(), structured_data(), readability() Meta tags and <link>s; JSON-LD, Open Graph and Twitter cards; the main article

Sensitive values read redacted, as for the MCP tools (Sensitive-field redaction). When the bridge cuts a read at its size cap (page text at 20,000 characters, HTML at 100 KB, Markdown at 80 KB), the method warns with a UserWarning; read a part of the page with a target instead.

evaluate runs in the extension's content-script world, not in the page's: it sees the page's DOM, and reaches the page's own JavaScript globals only through window.wrappedJSObject, so evaluate("() => window.wrappedJSObject.appState").

docs.title: Inspecting
docs.text:
Tab method Returns bounds(target) An element's box, the viewport and page sizes, and inView computed_style(target, properties=None) Computed CSS, a common set of properties by default explain_selector(selector) How many elements a CSS selector matches, samples, and more specific suggestions full_page_metrics() Document size, viewport, scroll position and device pixel ratio highlight(target), clear_highlight() Outline an element on the page watch_console(enabled=True), console_logs(since=None, level=None) Record the page's console, then read the messages network.start(), .requests(since=0), .stop(), .clear(), .resources() The page's requests from its resource timing (no headers or bodies); resources() needs no start()

browser.intercept blocks or redirects requests in every tab: add(patterns, effect="block") with URL regexes, rules(), log() and clear().

docs.title: Acting
docs.text:
Targets are a ref from snapshot() or find(), CSS, or one of the Playwright-style selectors such as text=Save or role=button[name="Save"]. A write's selector must match one element: otherwise it raises ambiguous_target and nothing runs, and first=True acts on the first match (Strict selectors).

Tab method Does navigate(url), back(), forward(), reload(bypass_cache=False) Navigate the tab click(target, button=None, modifiers=None, hold_ms=0), double_click(target), hover(target, duration_ms=0, steps=None) Pointer events (synthetic) on the target; hold_ms (0-10000) holds a click's press for long-press controls, and duration_ms (0-10000) or steps (1-50) keep a hover moving across the target for hover-intent controls (POST /api/click, POST /api/hover) fill(target, value) Replace a field's or editor's value type(target, text, clear=False) Type with key events fill_form(fields) Fill several fields; each key is a CSS selector, name, label or placeholder press(key, target=None, modifiers=None, text=None) Press "Enter", "ArrowDown", "a", ... with modifiers such as {"ctrl": True} select_option(target, value, by_text=False) Choose an <option> check(target, checked=True), uncheck(target) Set a checkbox or radio button scroll(direction="down", amount=500, target=None) Scroll the target or the window submit_form(target=None) Submit a form handle_dialogs(accept=True, prompt_text=None) Answer this tab's future dialogs; None leaves them to you again focus(target), blur(target=None) Move focus drag(source, destination) HTML5 drag events, else pointer events (via says which) insert(target, text, html=False, clear=False) Insert text into an editor, input or textarea, appending unless clear; html=True (developer build) inserts HTML into an editor upload_files(paths, target=None), drop(target, paths=None, data=None) Put local files into a file input, or drop files and data on an element trusted_click(target=None, x=0, y=0, coordinate_space="viewport", restore_pointer=True, button="left", click_count=1, modifiers=None, hold_ms=0) A click with the real OS pointer, for pages that ignore synthetic clicks; button="right"/"middle", click_count=2, modifiers=["Shift", ...] and hold_ms (a long press) choose the click. It moves your cursor for the click, then back unless restore_pointer=False, and may show the tab for the click (browser_trusted_click)

Actions return the bridge's result. ok: True only means the action was dispatched. To check what happened, pass expect, for example expect={"url_changed": True} or expect={"text": "Saved"}; an unmet outcome raises KitsuneError with code outcome_not_observed (Action outcomes). Pointer and typing actions also take wait=True to wait up to timeout ms for their target first (Actionability wait). Tabs an action opened are in its opened_tabs; open them with browser.tab(id). A menu, listbox or dialog that click, double_click or hover opened is in its opened_popup (Opened popups).

docs.title: Waiting
docs.text:
tab.wait_for(...) waits up to timeout ms (default 10000) for exactly one condition and raises TimedOut if it does not hold:

Condition Holds when target= the element is visible text=, text_gone= the rendered page text contains, or no longer contains, the literal text. Names from placeholders and aria-labels are not page text url=, title= the tab's URL or title matches a JavaScript regex; survives navigation js= an expression returns a non-empty result (developer build only) network_idle=True no new resource loaded for 500 ms

docs.title: Batches, parallel tabs and workflows
docs.text:
browser.batch(commands, tab=None) runs batch commands in one request, browser.parallel(sequences) runs one sequence per tab concurrently, and browser.workflow(name, variables) runs a named workflow (browser.workflows() lists them). A failed command does not raise: each one's outcome is in results and progress (Container progress). A call that did not finish ok returns call and resume_token for browser.resume(...) (Checkpoint and resume). browser.retry(command, max_attempts=3) repeats one command while it fails retryably.

For several tabs, browser.keep_alive(tabs) stops the browser's tab unloader from discarding them until stop_keep_alive(), browser.broadcast(tabs, command) runs one command in each, and browser.sync_barrier(tabs, predicate) waits until a JavaScript predicate holds in all of them.

docs.title: Browser data
docs.text:
Method Returns tab.local_storage, tab.session_storage: .get(key), .set(key, value), .remove(key), .clear(), .items() The page's storage browser.cookies.get(url=None, name=None, domain=None) Matching cookies browser.cookies.set(url, name, value, domain=None, path=None, secure=False), .remove(url, name), .clear(url=None, domain=None) The bridge's result browser.clipboard.read(), .write(text) The system clipboard browser.downloads.start(url, filename=None), .list(query=None), .cancel(download_id) A download id, the latest downloads browser.sessions.save(name, urls=None), .load(name), .list(), .delete(name) Cookies, and the localStorage of urls' origins, saved to disk by the bridge browser.clear_browsing_data(types, since=None) Remove the named kinds of data, such as ["cache"]. types is required: without it the extension would also remove cookies, history and saved passwords browser.history.search(query="", since=None, limit=20) Visited pages, newest first; since is a datetime (naive is local time) browser.history.visits(url) The visits to one URL from search browser.bookmarks.search(query="", limit=20) Matching bookmarks

With ask-before-act on, page storage, cookies, the clipboard and downloads raise ConfirmationRequired for every operation, reads included (Ask-before-act).

History and bookmarks need a browser permission that only you can grant, once, with Allow history and bookmarks on Kitsune's options page (about:addons → Kitsune → Options); until then they raise permission_required. Results stay inside the bridge's history scope (History and bookmarks).

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A failed result raises a KitsuneError. Its code, retryable, hint and state are the action error fields, and result is the whole reply. Branch on code, not on the message. retryable=False means a write may already have taken effect: check the page before repeating it. needs_user is the exception: nothing ran, and only you can let it go on.

Exception Raised for ConfirmationRequired An action that needs your approval (needs_user with state.reason approval, and a token), with token, expires_in, message and detail: confirmation_required (ask-before-act, with hold_reason), or user_tab (closing a user tab, from a v0.7.1 extension) ConnectionFailed (also a ConnectionError) The bridge or extension was not reached or dropped the request: the connection codes, bridge_disconnected and bridge_version_mismatch TimedOut (also a TimeoutError) timeout, a page load that timed out, and a wait that ran out KitsuneError Every other failure, such as stale_ref, ambiguous_target or outcome_not_observed

Warnings that accompany a success (warning) do not raise.

Until #376 these approvals had their own codes, confirmation_required and user_tab. They are now code needs_user, with the old code in state.detail (error.detail), and an ask-before-act hold's reason in state.holdReason (error.hold_reason, before: state.reason). ConfirmationRequired is raised for both shapes. A needs_user without a token, as in read and draft modes (state.approvable: false), raises a plain KitsuneError: nothing can approve it there.

docs.title: Ask-before-act
docs.text:
Some actions need your approval, and nothing runs until you give it: with ask-before-act on, the bridge holds submits, payment pages, JavaScript and cookie access (detail confirmation_required). User-tab writes instead fail immediately with user_tab_read_only; approval tokens do not override tab permissions. Actions needing approval raise ConfirmationRequired; error.message is a short request to show you. Repeat the call with confirm=error.token within error.expires_in seconds, or let connect(confirm=...) decide: the function gets the error, and when it returns True the action is sent once more with its token. In a script, that function can ask you, so the approval comes from a person. The Python API has no MCP elicitation, so it always gets the token, and the bridge's audit log records these approvals with approval: "token":

def ask(held):
    return input(f"{held} -- allow? [y/N] ").strip().lower() == "y"

browser = kitsune.connect(confirm=ask)

docs.title: The bridge
docs.text: Browser method Returns status(), version(), health() Connection state with its diagnosis, versions, and the bridge's own state logs(limit=200), audit(limit=100, since=None) The bridge's log lines; every client's commands from its audit log scheduler() Command scopes, pending commands and tab locks policy.get(), policy.set(allow=None, deny=None, readonly=None, ask=None, ask_urls=None, ...) The bridge's policy, for every client; a locked ask-before-act stays on cache(action="status", seconds=None), reload_extension() The read cache; reload the extension

docs.title: Any other route
docs.text: browser.request(route, body=None, timeout=15) sends any bridge route: GET without a body, POST with one. It raises the same errors and applies confirm. Tab routes take tabId in the body, for example browser.request("/api/full-page-metrics", {"tabId": tab.id}).

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
What the bridge protects against:

  • Web pages calling the local API. The HTTP API needs the bearer token and sends no CORS headers, so a page in the browser cannot use it.
  • DNS rebinding. Requests with a Host other than 127.0.0.1 / localhost are rejected.
  • Web pages posing as the extension. The WebSocket only accepts moz-extension:// origins. Before this check, any page could connect and take over the extension's slot.

What it does not protect against:

  • Prompt injection. A page the agent reads can contain instructions. The agent acts with every account you are logged into.
  • Local processes running as your user can read the token.
  • Sensitive page data. A connected agent can read page content and execute JavaScript in pages. Structural read tools (browser_snapshot, browser_forms, browser_dom, browser_query, browser_html, browser_find) redact password, one-time-code, card-number/CSC, secret-named, CSS-masked (including masked textareas and contenteditable regions) and autofilled fields, including web-component fields with a shadow root, and leave out CSS-masked static text. Selectors that probe a sensitive field's value attribute are refused; see Sensitive-field redaction. This is not a sandbox: browser_evaluate can read anything the page can, and the detection is heuristic. Do not assume a visually masked field is hidden from the agent or its logs.
  • Typed values outside the bridge. The bridge audit log (browser_audit) keeps the action, target, tab, timing and outcome of each write action but replaces typed text (browser_type, browser_fill_form values, browser_press_key text, browser_select_option values, browser_drop data and browser_handle_dialog prompt answers) and stored secrets (browser_cookies, browser_storage and browser_clipboard values) with "[redacted]"; see Audit log. The page and the MCP client's own transcript still see whatever the agent sent.
  • Cookies, page storage, saved sessions and the clipboard. Off unless you name the storage capability group; KITSUNE_CAPS=all leaves it out. Its tools read and write the cookies that keep you logged in, page storage and the system clipboard: enable it only for agents you trust with your accounts.
  • History and bookmarks. Off unless you enable the history capability group and allow it on Kitsune's options page (about:addons → Kitsune → Options); revoke it there or in the add-on's Permissions tab. Lookups return only URLs, titles, visit times and bookmark folders inside the bridge's history scope (by default the last 30 days), with token-like URL values replaced by [redacted], and every lookup is audited without its result URLs; see History and bookmarks. Titles and URLs can still be personal: enable it only for agents you trust with them.
  • Authenticated actions. Existing sessions let the agent act as you on accessible sites. MCP annotations are client hints, not an approval system. Ask-before-act holds actions for your approval. In the client's prompt (elicitation) the approval does not pass through the agent; the confirm token, the fallback for clients without elicitation, is an explicit second step, not human approval.

Kitsune does not provide a password-vault listing tool. Native password-manager autofill is browser-controlled; whether an autofilled value is accessible depends on what the browser makes available to the page. Test it only with disposable credentials, and never paste real secrets into bug reports.

Capability groups bound what an agent can reach through one MCP server, and the bridge checks them on every request, container steps included. They are not a sandbox: the kitsune-bridge command and other local programs with the token are not restricted.

Recommended: use a separate browser profile that only has the accounts the agent needs, and keep banking, mail and work SSO out of it. Enable only the capability groups you need, review the agent's actions, and treat saved sessions, screenshots, and tool logs as potentially sensitive.

docs.title: Tool list
docs.text:
Current tools defined in tools.py and playwright_tools.py and registered by server.py, grouped by capability. The default KITSUNE_CAPS=core exposes the 27 core tools: Playwright MCP's 25 core tools with the same definitions (Core tools), browser_resume and browser_ask_user. KITSUNE_CAPS=all exposes all 97. Set a comma-separated list to enable selected groups, for example KITSUNE_CAPS=core,browse,read. The storage and history groups are not part of all: they read personal data and must be named, as in KITSUNE_CAPS=all,storage,history. Calling a tool that is not published returns tool_not_published naming the setting (API reference). With KITSUNE_PUBLISH set to fewer groups, tools/list starts with those and the gateway tools below reach the rest (Finding tools without a restart).

These counts describe the default KITSUNE_MODE=act. KITSUNE_MODE=read|draft further intersects the capability surface and enforces the same limits on bridge calls; see Task modes. With core:

  • read (9): browser_tab_list, browser_navigate, browser_snapshot, browser_find, browser_wait_for, browser_console_messages, browser_network_requests, browser_network_request, browser_ask_user.
  • draft (12): read plus browser_type, browser_select_option, browser_fill_form.
  • Other enabled groups contribute only read tools (browse adds browser_scroll and, for draft, browser_check). Restricted modes replace multi-action browser_tabs with browser_tab_list, which lists tabs and opens background tabs (new_tab) but cannot close or select them, and omit clicks, submit, JavaScript, screenshots/file writes, policy changes and containers. Draft refuses sensitive/payment-like fills without issuing confirmation tokens.

See the API reference for parameters and behavior.

docs.title: Tools, capabilities and modes
docs.text:
By default Kitsune publishes the 25 tools of Playwright MCP's default capabilities, with the same names, descriptions, input schemas and annotations, as its core capability group (see Core tools), with Kitsune's browser_resume, which continues a call that stopped for you, and browser_ask_user, with which the agent asks you for what it cannot do (#376). Kitsune's other tools are in the other groups. Set KITSUNE_CAPS in the MCP server environment before starting it; restart the MCP client after changing it. The comma-separated list selects exactly those groups (include core to retain the default tools). all enables all 97 tools in every group except storage and history, which read personal data and must be named (KITSUNE_CAPS=all,storage,history). Whitespace and case are ignored; unknown group names fail at startup.

[mcp_servers.kitsune.env]
KITSUNE_CAPS = "core,browse,read"
Group Tools for browse Scrolling, forward navigation, checkboxes, focus, form submits, real mouse clicks read Page text and Markdown, forms, DOM, links, images, metadata inspect Element bounds, computed styles, selector checks, highlights tabs Pinning, muting, zoom, windows, tab tags, keep-alive automation Batches, retries, workflows, parallel tabs, and resuming an interrupted batch network Downloads, request interception and capture admin Connection status, logs, audit, cache, policy storage, history Cookies, page storage, clipboard and saved sessions; history and bookmarks. These read personal data, so all leaves them out and you name them yourself

The tool list names every tool in each group.

Earlier releases' devtools, parallel, windows and session groups are gone, and naming them fails at startup. devtools became browse, read, inspect, admin and (browser_workflows, browser_workflow) automation; parallel became automation and, for tab tags and keep-alive, tabs; windows joined tabs; session joined storage, which all no longer includes.

A tool left out by KITSUNE_CAPS is absent from tools/list, and clients usually say nothing about it. Calling it anyway returns an MCP error with code: "tool_not_published" whose hint names the setting that publishes it, for example KITSUNE_CAPS=browse,core for browser_scroll. browser_status (admin) reports this server's mcp_tools: the enabled caps, how many known tools are unpublished, and its audit client and tab owner ids.

The bridge enforces the groups too. The MCP server sends its enabled groups with every request, and the bridge refuses a route or a container step (of browser_batch, browser_parallel, browser_retry, browser_broadcast, browser_workflow or browser_resume) that belongs to another group with code: "capability_restricted". So automation runs only commands of the groups you enabled: with KITSUNE_CAPS=core,automation, a batch cookies step is refused until you add storage, and a workflow needs the groups of its steps. Like task modes, this limits what an agent can do through this MCP server; it is not a boundary against other local programs that hold the bridge token.

docs.title: Finding tools without a restart
docs.text:
KITSUNE_CAPS decides which tools this server runs. KITSUNE_PUBLISH decides which of them tools/list shows when a session starts; unset, it is KITSUNE_CAPS, so nothing changes. Set it to fewer groups to keep the list small and let the agent reach the rest in the same connection:

[mcp_servers.kitsune.env]
KITSUNE_CAPS = "all"
KITSUNE_PUBLISH = "core"

With Claude Code:

claude mcp add --scope user kitsune -e KITSUNE_CAPS=all -e KITSUNE_PUBLISH=core -- uvx --from kitsune-browser-mcp kitsune

tools/list then has the 27 core tools and three gateway tools:

  • browser_tools_search(query, limit=5) finds the tools this server runs but does not list, best match first, each with its full description, input schema and annotations. An empty query lists their names by group.
  • browser_tools_call(name, arguments) runs one and returns its own result, images included, and its error status.
  • browser_tools_publish(names) adds tools, or whole groups, to this session's tools/list and sends notifications/tools/list_changed; clients that refresh on it can then call them directly.

KITSUNE_PUBLISH takes the group names KITSUNE_CAPS does, and only groups KITSUNE_CAPS enables: naming another one fails at startup. The gateway tools appear only when some enabled tool is not published.

The gateway never runs more than a direct call could. It finds and runs only tools KITSUNE_CAPS and KITSUNE_MODE permit: all still leaves out storage and history unless named, and a name it does not permit gets the same tool_not_published as a direct call. A call through browser_tools_call takes the direct call's path, so argument validation, the task mode, confirmation tokens, protected user tabs, redaction and file name roots apply the same way, and its audit entries record via: {"gateway": "browser_tools_call", "tool": …}. Your client's permission prompt may show only browser_tools_call and its conservative annotations (destructive, open-world), not the tool it runs, so do not rely on per-tool client prompts for these calls. browser_tools_publish changes only that session's list, never what the server permits or another session's list. Clients differ in whether they act on notifications/tools/list_changed; the notification is not proof that the model sees the new tools, and browser_tools_call works either way.

This reaches tools that are already installed. Changing KITSUNE_CAPS or upgrading Kitsune still needs a restart.

The Kitsune-owned tools take tab_id to target background tabs; without it they act on the current tab like the core tools. They share an action contract (ref, wait, expect, confirm_token, first; confirm_token is the approval fallback for clients without elicitation) documented on browser_check; see the API reference and the tool list.

Every tool includes MCP annotations. The core tools carry Playwright MCP's; the Kitsune-owned ones have a human-readable title and read-only, destructive, idempotent, and open-world hints, annotated for their most dangerous operation. Clients can use these hints to inform permission prompts; enforcement depends on the client. The hints are not enforced policy. The bridge enforces task-mode limits and browser_set_policy (readonly, allow/deny, and ask-before-act).

docs.title: Core tools
docs.text:
The core tools other than browser_resume and browser_ask_user are Playwright MCP's, published verbatim from src/kitsune/playwright_tools.json (captured from @playwright/mcp with node scripts/update_playwright_tools.mjs), so a client or prompt written for Playwright MCP works unchanged. They drive your own browser through the Kitsune extension and return Kitsune's compact JSON results, not Playwright's Markdown. Where the two differ:

  • Current tab. Tools act on the tab browser_tabs new or select made current; select does not switch your view. It takes any tab, yours and other clients' too, so the agent can read it; on a tab it cannot write, the result says read_only: true. Kitsune's own tools called without tab_id, and browser_batch, browser_retry and browser_workflow commands that name no tabId, act on the current tab too. Until there is one, reads act on the active tab, and writes and navigations that name no tab return no_current_tab without sending anything (No current tab). An MCP server that restarts starts without a current tab; its no_current_tab then lists the open tabs its MCP client opened before, the most recent first, in state.ownTabs, and the hint names that tab, so the agent can pass it as tab_id (to a core tool, which takes none, the hint names its browser_tabs index to select). The server does not pick one itself: the tab may belong to an earlier conversation. Persistent ownership survives bridge/extension restarts and browser session restore for the same client id; handed-off tabs return when their session ends (Tab owners). A tab a batch or workflow newTab opens, or an action on the current tab opens (a click on a target=_blank link, for example), becomes current, and the result names it in current_tab. browser_navigate and browser_navigate_back also accept a tab_id that Playwright MCP's schema does not list. index is the position in browser_tabs list, which also marks active and agent-owned tabs, and the current one regardless of ownership. Selection does not grant ownership (Protecting your tabs). new, select and close return the tabs after the change in the same form; new returns the new tab's index. browser_close closes the current tab, never the browser; closing a user or other client's tab is refused with user_tab_read_only by default.
  • Targets. target is a snapshot ref (e12) or a CSS selector. Actions require one actionable match (else ambiguous_target). Actions and scoped snapshots also accept a subset of Playwright selectors: text= (also /regex/), role=…[name="…"] (also [name=/regex/]), internal:text=, internal:role=, internal:label=, :has-text(), :text-is(), :text(), :visible, CSS lists, >> chains (also starting at a ref, as in e12 >> xpath=..), nth=N and xpath= (refused on pages holding redacted content); see Target selectors. Unsupported forms return unsupported_selector with a hint, not a retryable missing target. Element screenshots use the same resolver and capture the exact selected node, including inside shadow roots. Refs survive newer observations while their nodes remain attached in the same document; navigation or replacement nodes require new refs.
  • Snapshots. Default core snapshots include redacted static text and resolved HTTP(S) link URLs (same-origin ones as paths; a link repeating the previous sibling link's URL, or, first under its parent, the page's, has no /url line). Returned inline they are capped at 12,000 characters, cut between blocks so a product card or paragraph is never split (a long navigation, banner or footer outside main is shown as its line and a … not shown marker until main is listed), with truncated: true and a hint toward browser_find, a scoped target or filename (which saves the whole snapshot; see browser_snapshot). Existing line clipping, structural collapsing and depth rules still apply: past the fifth of a run of similar items the snapshot shows - … N more similar items; snapshot e14 to list all when that hides at least three items (a run of up to seven is listed in full), and a snapshot with target e14 (the items' container) lists up to 100 of them. browser_find searches collapsed items too. In the full toolset, text=False is compact and text=True enables explicitly bounded readable output (12,000 final public chars). Explicit HTTP maxChars and post-action limits also apply after URL redaction; scoped snapshots remain useful for large pages.
  • Sliders and repeated keys. browser_fill_form type: "slider" and browser_type (without slowly) set a native <input type=range> directly. An ARIA slider or spinbutton (role=slider or spinbutton with a numeric aria-valuenow and no native input, the usual custom widget) is set as a user would: the extension focuses it and presses arrow keys (Home/End for an end) until its aria-valuenow is the value, all in one call, and returns the final value. If the value is outside aria-valuemin/aria-valuemax, the call fails with value_not_reached before any key; if it is not reached (the steps skip it, the widget stops moving, or 1,000 keys or 20 s run out) it fails the same way with state.value (Action errors). browser_press_key also accepts a repeat count (1–100) that Playwright MCP's schema does not list; the extension presses the key that many times in one call, a task apart.
  • Dialogs. browser_handle_dialog sets how the current tab answers its next dialogs (Firefox answers dialogs synchronously, so one already open cannot be answered).
  • Uploads and drops. A synthetic click opens no file chooser, so browser_file_upload fills the file input last clicked (or the input inside it, else the page's only file input). browser_drop fires dragenter/dragover/drop with the files and data.
  • JavaScript. browser_evaluate needs the developer extension build and runs in the content-script context; the result is JSON-parsed.
  • Console and network. browser_console_messages starts capture on first use, so earlier messages are missed. browser_network_requests lists the page's resource timing entries since it loaded; there are no headers or bodies, so browser_network_request with part answers not_supported.
  • Screenshots. browser_take_screenshot returns an inline image; filename saves PNG or JPEG. type chooses the encoding; otherwise .jpg/.jpeg filenames infer JPEG, with PNG as the default. Other formats answer not_supported; scale is ignored.
  • Not supported. browser_emulate_media and browser_run_code_unsafe are listed but answer not_supported (retryable: false): an extension cannot override CSS media features, and there is no Playwright page to run code against.
  • File names. A relative filename is resolved against KITSUNE_OUTPUT_DIR if set, else the first file:// root the MCP client lists (MCP roots, asked for on each call with a filename; no answer within 5 seconds counts as none), else the MCP server's working directory. Absolute names and ~ are used as given. saved_to is the absolute path written.

Ask-before-act holds still apply. On a client with elicitation the MCP server asks the user and repeats a held call itself (see Approving held actions). The core schemas have no confirm_token, the fallback for clients without elicitation; the tools accept it anyway, so on such a client, after the user approves a held action, an agent can repeat the call with confirm_token from the needs_user error.

docs.title: Task modes
docs.text:
Set KITSUNE_MODE=read|draft|act in the MCP server environment and restart the client. The default is act, preserving the existing tool surface and bridge policy. Mode names ignore case and surrounding whitespace; unknown names fail at startup.

[mcp_servers.kitsune.env]
KITSUNE_MODE = "read"
Mode Published tools and enforced limits read Read tools plus navigation to HTTP(S) pages (or about:blank) and scrolling. browser_tab_list replaces the multi-action browser_tabs; with new_tab it opens a background tab that later calls act on. It cannot close or select tabs. No clicks, field writes, JavaScript, submits, confirmations or screenshots/file writes. draft Read surface plus browser_type, browser_select_option, browser_fill_form and, with the browse group, browser_check. Fills plain text only; no click/keypress/submit/dialog confirmation or JavaScript. Ask-before-act is forced: sensitive fields, payment-like pages and uninspectable targets are refused before filling, without a confirmation token. act Existing behavior, including the independently configured ask-before-act policy.

Modes intersect with KITSUNE_CAPS; they never enable a disabled group. With the default core group, read publishes eight tools: list-only tabs, navigate, snapshot, find, wait for text, console messages and the network request list and details. draft adds type, select-option and fill-form. Page text, forms and DOM need the read group, and scrolling the browse group. Extra enabled groups contribute only their read tools. The personal-data storage and history groups still require explicit opt-in.

Restricted surfaces use first-paragraph descriptions and omit confirm_token, the approval fallback for clients without elicitation: they cannot approve. Calling an unpublished tool by name returns tool_not_published with the mode setting needed to publish it; browser_status.mcp_tools.mode identifies a restricted server. The gateway tools are listed in every mode and reach only the tools the mode permits. The bridge enforces the mode on every request, including calls made by name or directly over HTTP. A restricted request cannot change policy, run containers or resume an act call. Draft form-fill inspects every target before writing any field.

Modes are per MCP client: a read client cannot loosen its mode by calling browser_set_policy, and does not change another client's policy on the shared daemon. The bridge's existing URL/readonly/locked-ask policy can tighten the mode further. Use an act client or the browser itself for a sensitive action. Modes limit agent commands, not page scripts: navigation can still trigger site behavior and field events can autosave a draft. They are not an incognito session or an application-level sandbox. Exact token counts and research/account-lookup task measurements belong to kitsune-benchmark; character-size guards in this repo are not token measurements.

Run uvx --from kitsune-browser-mcp kitsune-bridge status in a terminal to see uv's error First start times out in the client Run uvx --from kitsune-browser-mcp kitsune-bridge status once to fill the uv cache, then reconnect uv cannot find kitsune-browser-mcp Check that PyPI is reachable (or your configured index mirrors it) uv cannot fetch a git+https:// source Check that git is installed and on the client's PATH, and that GitHub is reachable An upgrade is not picked up Restart the MCP client; then refresh with uvx --refresh … (see Upgrading) The bridge restarts every time a different client starts Clients use different sources or refs (see compatibility) extension_connected: false Extension installed and enabled in about:addons? With the developer build, the browser restarted, so the temporary add-on is gone?
